name: Human arm and hand (right, anterior view)

landmarks.note: MediaPipe Pose (right arm; use 11/13/15 for the left) + MediaPipe Hand Landmarker. Each part spans from -> to, as a fraction t along that segment.

parts.name: skin
parts.summary: The outer layer that protects everything underneath
parts.details: Epidermis and dermis over subcutaneous fat; dorsal hand veins are easily seen through it.

parts.name: deltoid
parts.summary: The rounded shoulder muscle that lifts your arm out to the side
parts.details: Origin: clavicle, acromion, spine of scapula. Insertion: deltoid tuberosity of humerus. Main abductor of the shoulder (15-90 degrees).

parts.name: biceps brachii
parts.summary: The front of the upper arm: bends the elbow and turns the palm up
parts.details: Two heads (long and short) from the scapula. Insertion: radial tuberosity and bicipital aponeurosis. Strongest supinator; flexes the elbow, especially when the forearm is supinated.

parts.name: triceps brachii
parts.summary: The back of the upper arm: straightens the elbow
parts.details: Long, lateral and medial heads. Insertion: olecranon of ulna. The main elbow extensor.

parts.name: brachioradialis
parts.summary: Runs along the thumb side of the forearm: helps bend the elbow
parts.details: Origin: lateral supracondylar ridge of humerus. Insertion: radial styloid. Strongest in elbow flexion with the forearm mid-prone (thumb up, like holding a mug).

parts.name: forearm flexor group
parts.summary: The muscles on the palm side of the forearm: bend the wrist and fingers
parts.details: Superficial group from the medial epicondyle (common flexor origin): pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, flexor carpi ulnaris, flexor digitorum superficialis. Deep: flexor digitorum profundus, flexor pollicis longus.
parts.nerve: mostly median nerve; flexor carpi ulnaris and medial half of FDP by ulnar nerve
parts.safety: Overuse at the common flexor origin is 'golfer's elbow' (medial epicondylitis).

parts.name: forearm extensor group
parts.summary: The muscles on the back of the forearm: straighten the wrist and fingers
parts.details: From the lateral epicondyle (common extensor origin): extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi, extensor carpi ulnaris.
parts.safety: Overuse at the common extensor origin is 'tennis elbow' (lateral epicondylitis).

parts.name: thenar muscles
parts.summary: The fleshy pad at the base of the thumb: lets you touch thumb to fingers
parts.details: Abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis. Opposition of the thumb is key to precision grip.
parts.safety: Wasting here can be a sign of carpal tunnel syndrome.

parts.name: hypothenar muscles
parts.summary: The pad on the little-finger side of the palm
parts.details: Abductor digiti minimi, flexor digiti minimi brevis, opponens digiti minimi.

parts.name: brachialis
parts.summary: Lies under the biceps: the main elbow bender
parts.details: Origin: distal anterior humerus. Insertion: coronoid process and ulnar tuberosity. The pure, workhorse elbow flexor in any forearm position.
parts.nerve: musculocutaneous nerve (small lateral part by radial nerve)

parts.name: pronator teres and pronator quadratus
parts.summary: Turn the palm to face down, and hold it there while you type
parts.details: Pronator teres runs from the medial epicondyle to the mid-radius; pronator quadratus is a square muscle across the distal radius and ulna and is the main pronator. Typing keeps the forearm pronated, so they hold steadily.
parts.nerve: median nerve (quadratus via the anterior interosseous branch)

parts.name: interossei and lumbricals
parts.summary: Small muscles between the hand bones: spread and close the fingers
parts.details: Dorsal interossei abduct (DAB), palmar interossei adduct (PAD). Lumbricals flex the MCP joints and extend the IP joints.
parts.nerve: ulnar nerve; lumbricals 1-2 by median nerve

parts.name: finger flexor tendons
parts.summary: White cords that pull the fingers closed
parts.details: They pass through the carpal tunnel with the median nerve. FDS inserts on the middle phalanx and splits to let FDP pass through to the distal phalanx.

parts.name: finger extensor tendons
parts.summary: Cords on the back of the hand that straighten the fingers
parts.details: Extensor digitorum tendons fan out over the back of the hand into the extensor expansions (dorsal hoods) of each finger.

parts.name: median nerve
parts.summary: The main nerve to the forearm flexors and the thumb side of the hand
parts.details: Runs down the arm with the brachial artery and through the carpal tunnel. Supplies sensation to the palmar thumb, index, middle and half the ring finger.
parts.safety: Compression at the wrist is carpal tunnel syndrome.

parts.name: ulnar nerve
parts.summary: The 'funny bone' nerve: supplies the little-finger side of the hand
parts.details: Passes behind the medial epicondyle, then into the hand. Supplies most small muscles of the hand.

parts.name: radial nerve
parts.summary: Supplies the muscles that straighten the elbow, wrist and fingers
parts.details: Winds around the back of the humerus in the radial groove; its posterior interosseous branch supplies the forearm extensors.
parts.safety: A mid-shaft humerus fracture can injure it, causing wrist drop.

parts.name: brachial, radial and ulnar arteries
parts.summary: Carry blood down the arm; the radial artery is where you feel a pulse at the wrist
parts.details: The brachial artery splits at the elbow into the radial and ulnar arteries, which join in the hand as the palmar arches.

parts.name: humerus
parts.summary: The upper arm bone
parts.details: Head articulates with the glenoid; the medial and lateral epicondyles at the elbow anchor the forearm flexors and extensors.

parts.name: radius and ulna
parts.summary: The two forearm bones; they cross over when you turn your palm down
parts.details: Radius on the thumb side, ulna on the little-finger side. In pronation the radius rotates over the ulna.

parts.name: carpals, metacarpals and phalanges
parts.summary: 27 bones: 8 wrist bones, 5 palm bones and 14 finger bones
parts.details: Carpals: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate. Each finger has 3 phalanges; the thumb has 2.
parts.safety: Pain in the anatomical snuffbox after a fall can mean a scaphoid fracture.
parts.procedural_fallback_note: fal drew the distal phalanx wrong twice; it is a simple shape built in code (scripts/arm/procedural.ts).

steps.text: This arm is typing. On the surface you only see small finger taps.
Peel back the skin: the real work is in the forearm. The flexors press each key, the extensors lift the fingers back up.
Deeper: the pronators keep the palm facing down, and the small hand muscles spread and steady the fingers.
The tendons are the puppet strings: watch the one for each finger slide as it presses a key.
The median nerve shares the carpal tunnel with those tendons, which is why heavy typing is linked to carpal tunnel syndrome.
Underneath it all: the radius and ulna are crossed over because the forearm is turned palm-down.

typing.how_detected: Both: forearm pronated (palm facing down) AND fingertips making small, quick up-down taps (about 2-10 per second) while the wrist stays fairly still.
typing.summary: Typing looks gentle, but it uses the forearm far more than the hand. Most of the finger-moving muscles live in your forearm and pull on long tendons, like puppet strings.

roles.role: Flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus press each key down by pulling the flexor tendons
Transmit each keypress through the carpal tunnel to the fingertip; the tendon for the finger that pressed slides
Lift each finger back off the key, and hold the wrist steady in slight extension (extensor carpi radialis brevis works hard here)
Pull each finger back up after the press
Fine control: spread the fingers to reach keys and keep the fingertips curved
Hold the palm facing down the whole time
Small, steady work holding the arm in position
Minimal: elbow held at about 90 degrees
Minimal: elbow held at about 90 degrees

typing.clinical_note: Long hours of typing are linked to repetitive strain: lateral epicondylitis (overuse of the extensor origin, especially ECRB) and carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve compression where the flexor tendons and the nerve share the tunnel). Educational, not medical advice.
